This is a simple series circuit diagram. At the left side you have a 6‑volt battery, shown with a positive and a negative terminal. Moving clockwise the battery is connected to a switch that is in the open position; the lever is not touching the two terminals, so no current can pass through it at the moment.

Below the switch, at the bottom of the loop, are two resistors. The first one, labeled R1, has a value of 10 ohms. To its right, still on the bottom line, is the second resistor, R2, which is 20 ohms. The layout places R1 to the right of R2, with the switch positioned above the loop and the battery on the far left.

Because the switch is open, the circuit is incomplete and no current flows. If the switch were closed, the two resistors would be in series: their resistances would add to a total of 30 ohms, and with the 6‑volt source the current would be 0.2 amperes, following Ohm’s law. But as drawn, the open switch stops any current from moving through the resistors.
What will happen if i increase voltage

If the switch stays open, nothing will change when you turn the battery’s voltage up. The circuit is still broken, so no current can flow through the resistors, no matter how high the voltage is.

If you close the switch, the two resistors are in series. Their total resistance is 10 ohms plus 20 ohms, which is 30 ohms. In that case Ohm’s law tells us that the current will be the voltage divided by 30 ohms. So if you double the battery voltage, the current will double; if you triple it, the current will triple.

Because the power a resistor dissipates is the square of the voltage across it divided by its resistance, increasing the supply voltage also increases the power in each resistor. With a higher voltage, each resistor will get warmer and may heat up more quickly. If the voltage becomes too large, the resistors could overheat or even burn out, and the battery might get stressed as well.

So, to sum up: with the switch open, raising the voltage does nothing. With the switch closed, the current grows linearly with the voltage, and the power—and thus heating—in the resistors grows with the square of the voltage.
